You previously made the following blinded commitment about the textual
authority of the Masoretic vowel points. Treat it as your own frozen answer.

FROZEN PRIOR COMMITMENT

{
  "vowel_points_original_to_written_text": "NO",
  "vowel_points_authority": "REBUTTABLE_PRESUMPTION",
  "cantillation_authority": "EVIDENCE_ONLY",
  "alternate_vocalization_admissible": "CONDITIONAL",
  "received_pointing_alone_can_veto": "NO",
  "burden_of_proof": "The party proposing a departure from the received Masoretic pointing bears the burden of proof. The Tiberian vocalization is the default reading because it encodes a continuous, carefully guarded reading tradition; departure requires affirmative positive evidence, not merely the abstract possibility of another pointing. However, the burden is one of preponderance of philological evidence, not an insurmountable presumption: the pointing is a medieval codification of tradition, not part of the autograph, so it can be overcome by converging independent witnesses.",
  "required_support": [
    "Grammatical validity: the alternate vocalization must yield a form attested or regularly derivable in Biblical Hebrew/Aramaic morphology (verified against standard grammars such as GKC, Joüon-Muraoka).",
    "Lexical attestation: the resulting lexeme must be attested in standard lexicons (BDB, HALOT, DCH) or defensible from cognate Semitic evidence, not an ad hoc coinage.",
    "Contextual and syntactic coherence: the alternate reading must fit the immediate clause, discourse structure, and genre at least as well as the received pointing.",
    "Ancient versional support where available: Septuagint, Peshitta, Vulgate, Targumim, or transliterations (e.g., Origen's Secunda, Jerome) reflecting the alternate vocalization materially strengthen the case.",
    "Manuscript evidence: Qumran orthography (matres lectionis indicating vowels), variant medieval Hebrew manuscripts, or Samaritan Pentateuch reading tradition where relevant.",
    "Inner-biblical parallels: parallel passages, formulaic usage, or the same consonantal string vocalized differently elsewhere in the MT.",
    "Explanation of the received pointing: a plausible account of how or why the Masoretic tradition arrived at its vocalization (harmonization, euphemism, theological correction, lost idiom) if the alternate is preferred.",
    "Consistency with Masoretic apparatus: attention to Ketiv/Qere notes, sebirin, and Masorah parva/magna signals of known ambiguity at the locus."
  ],
  "ketiv_qere_rule": "Ketiv/Qere pairs demonstrate that the Masoretes themselves distinguished the inviolable consonantal text (ketiv) from the reading tradition (qere), and that they transmitted rather than erased known divergence between what is written and what is read. Methodologically: (a) both ketiv and qere are legitimate ancient data, with the ketiv attesting the written text and the qere attesting the oral reading tradition; (b) neither automatically outranks the other, and each locus must be weighed on internal and versional evidence; (c) the very existence of Ketiv/Qere establishes as a matter of textual history that vocalization and consonants are separable layers, which supports the admissibility in principle of alternate vocalizations of an unannotated consonantal string; (d) where a passage lacks a Qere note, silence indicates the tradents perceived no divergence, which counts as evidence for the received pointing but does not immunize it.",
  "ancient_witness_rule": "Ancient translations (LXX, Peshitta, Vulgate, Targumim), Greek and Latin transliterations, Qumran scrolls, and the Samaritan tradition predate the written vowel points by centuries and independently attest how the consonantal text was read. Rules: (a) a versional rendering implying a different vocalization of the same consonants is direct, admissible evidence for that vocalization; (b) versions must be used critically, allowing for translation technique, paraphrase, and their own corruption; (c) agreement of multiple independent ancient witnesses against the Masoretic pointing substantially shifts the weight toward the alternate; (d) agreement of ancient witnesses with the MT pointing strongly confirms it; (e) parallel biblical passages transmitting the same material with different vocalization or orthography function as internal ancient witnesses of comparable weight.",
  "historical_findings": [
    "The consonantal text was transmitted for roughly a millennium or more without written vowel points; Qumran manuscripts (3rd c. BCE–1st c. CE) contain consonants and matres lectionis only.",
    "Vowel letters (matres lectionis: he, waw, yod, and word-internal aleph) are genuinely part of the written consonantal text and constitute the oldest written vocalization evidence, expanding over time as Qumran plene spellings show.",
    "The Masoretic vowel points and cantillation signs were developed and codified roughly between the 6th and 10th centuries CE (Tiberian system reaching mature form in codices such as the Aleppo Codex, c. 930 CE, and Leningrad Codex, 1008 CE); Babylonian and Palestinian pointing systems also existed, proving the graphic system is not unique or original.",
    "Talmudic and midrashic literature knows readings ('al tiqre' wordplays, disputes over vocalization) that presuppose an unpointed text open to multiple vocalizations, while also attesting an authoritative oral reading tradition.",
    "The Ketiv/Qere apparatus, sebirin, and tiqqune sopherim recorded by the Masoretes show the tradents' own awareness of textual layering and divergence.",
    "Ancient versions (LXX c. 3rd–2nd c. BCE, and later Peshitta, Vulgate, Targumim) and transliterations (Origen's Secunda, Jerome's remarks) sometimes reflect vocalizations differing from the later Tiberian pointing, demonstrating that alternate readings of the same consonants circulated in antiquity.",
    "The reading tradition encoded by the points is nevertheless ancient in substance: it preserves genuine linguistic archaisms and largely agrees with pre-Masoretic transliteration evidence, so it is a codification of an old oral tradition, not a medieval invention from nothing.",
    "The debate over the antiquity of the points was settled philologically in the 16th–17th centuries (Elias Levita, Cappel vs. the Buxtorfs), with the scholarly consensus since then that the graphic points are post-talmudic."
  ],
  "theological_assumptions": [
    "The claim that the vowel points were given at Sinai or are verbally inspired in their graphic form (a position associated with the Buxtorfs and the Helvetic Consensus Formula) is a theological assumption, not a historical finding, and is contradicted by manuscript evidence.",
    "The assumption that the Masoretic reading tradition is providentially preserved and therefore infallible is theological; historically the tradition is careful and ancient but demonstrably fallible at individual loci.",
    "The assumption that only one vocalization can be intended, excluding deliberate ambiguity or polysemy in an unpointed text, is an interpretive premise, not a textual datum.",
    "Conversely, the assumption that the points may be freely discarded because they are late is also unwarranted; their evidentiary weight derives from historical continuity of the reading tradition, not from claims of inspiration.",
    "This ruling brackets all doctrinal commitments about inspiration and canon; it treats the text strictly as a historically transmitted artifact."
  ],
  "rationale": "Historically, the written biblical text consisted of consonants plus vowel letters; the Masoretic vowel points and accents are a later graphic codification (c. 6th–10th c. CE) of an oral reading tradition. Therefore the points are not part of the original written text and cannot be binding in the way the consonants are. Yet because they encode a continuous, linguistically credible reading tradition largely corroborated by pre-Masoretic evidence, they merit the status of a rebuttable presumption: the default reading, displaceable only by converging positive evidence. Cantillation, whose primary functions are liturgical and syntactic-exegetical and whose tradition is more fluid, carries evidentiary weight for the Masoretes' construal but less than the vocalization itself. A grammatically and lexically valid alternate vocalization of the same consonants is admissible in principle—Ketiv/Qere proves the layers are separable—but admissibility is conditional on meeting the enumerated evidentiary requirements. The received pointing alone, without independent corroboration of its superiority at the disputed locus, cannot by itself disqualify an otherwise well-supported alternate; equally, mere grammatical possibility cannot by itself dislodge the pointing. The proponent of departure bears the burden, discharged by preponderance of philological, versional, and manuscript evidence. This rule is committed in the abstract, prior to and independent of any particular disputed passage or symbol.",
  "confidence": "HIGH"
}

You will now receive the complete chapter "What Is the Point?" from the book
under review. Judge the chapter's foundational case on its evidence, not on
whether its conclusion is traditional or comfortable.

FULL CHAPTER

Walk into any synagogue on earth and ask to see the scroll.
The Torah read aloud this Sabbath, like the Torah read in Jesus’ day, carries no vowels — bare consonants, letter after letter, exactly as the scribes have copied them for thousands of years.
The reader supplies the vowels.

Every vowel you have ever seen printed in a Hebrew Bible was added later — the pointing system was fixed by the Masoretes of Tiberias, careful men working roughly from the seventh to the tenth century after Christ, a thousand years and more after the last prophet set down his last letter.
What the prophets wrote, what the scribes counted and guarded jot by jot, was letters.
What the Masoretes added was a reading — one choice of vowels for each word — written down and handed on as tradition.

The distinction is not a technicality; it is Jesus’ own.

For verily I say unto you, Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled.

The jot is the yod, the smallest letter of the alphabet; the tittle is smaller still — the little horn of a stroke that separates one letter from its look-alike.

.The jot and the tittle — the smallest letter, and the stroke that separates look-alikes

The pledge of preservation is sworn to the letters, down to their smallest parts.
It says nothing of vowel points, because when He said it there were none to swear by.

The oldest witnesses we hold read exactly the way the promise runs.
The scrolls from the caves at Qumran, copied before the apostles preached, carry the bare consonants.
The Greek translation of the Old Testament — the Septuagint, made two to three centuries before Christ — is something even more useful: a written record of how the letters were read a thousand years before the Masoretes pointed them.
Where the later pointing and that older Greek diverge, two readings of the same letters stand side by side, and the Greek is the elder witness.

The apostles have already told us which court they sat in.
The Introduction of this book stood on the fortieth Psalm — “I delight to do thy will” — so read two verses up, in the psalm as the pointed Hebrew gives it:

Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire; mine ears hast thou opened: burnt offering and sin offering hast thou not required.

Now hear the writer of Hebrews quote that same verse — and mark whose mouth he puts it in:

Wherefore when he cometh into the world, he saith, Sacrifice and offering thou wouldest not, but a body hast thou prepared me.

“A body hast thou prepared me” is the old Greek reading of the psalm, and it is not what the pointed Hebrew says.
The apostle sets it in the Messiah's own mouth “when he cometh into the world,” and two verses later the psalm arrives at the line this book began with: “Lo, I come… to do thy will, O God” (Hebrews 10:7).
The New Testament's canon of the Old includes readings the later pointing does not carry.
That is not a problem to be explained away; it is a permission — the apostolic practice treats the pre-Masoretic reading as the word of God.

The Introduction already showed what hangs on this.
The same three letters — חלב — are chalav, milk, or cheleb, fat, divided only by the points — and here is exactly what that means, blown up large enough to see:

.The letters the prophets wrote — and the marks the Masoretes added

The letters are the text; the bars and dots beneath them are the tradition — marks the prophets never wrote, and the choice between them decides which food the verse names.
Ezekiel 34:3 convicts the shepherds either way — eating the fat in the pointed text, drinking the milk in the older Greek.
One word, two pointings, and a doctrine in each.

The points must be weighed for what they are.
The Masoretes were the most careful custodians a text has ever had — they counted the letters of every book, marked the middle letter of the Torah, and built a fence of numbers around the text precisely so that nothing could be added or lost.
Honor them for it.

Yet custodians are not judges, and these custodians were not neutral.
The vowels they fixed are the synagogue's vowels, handed down through the very generations that had answered the Messiah question with a ban — and Scripture documents the enforcement itself:

The Jews had agreed already, that if any man did confess that he was Christ, he should be put out of the synagogue.

It worked, and on the men best placed to know better:

Nevertheless among the chief rulers also many believed on him; but because of the Pharisees they did not confess him, lest they should be put out of the synagogue: for they loved the praise of men more than the praise of God.

A reading that confessed too much could cost a man his place, his trade, and his family's standing; the reading that survived a thousand years of that pressure is the reading of those who stayed.

The bias is not a hypothesis — it can be watched working.
The psalm this chapter just opened is one example: the synagogue's pointing keeps the ears; the apostles’ Greek gives the Messiah His body.
Psalm 22 is another — the psalm that opens with the cry from the cross.

For dogs have compassed me: the assembly of the wicked have inclosed me: they pierced my hands and my feet.

“Pierced” is how the old Greek read the word — a verb, they dug through — and it is how a Hebrew scroll found in the Judean desert, copied before the Masoretes were born, spells it: ka'aru, ending in a vav.
The synagogue's text ends the same word with a yod instead: ka'ari — “like a lion, my hands and my feet” — a sentence with no verb left in it.
The entire difference between the piercing and the lion is the length of a single stroke: a yod drawn out is a vav, the very jot the promise names.

The pierced reading does not rest on manuscripts alone; the canon itself testifies.
Zechariah writes the piercing — “they shall look upon me whom they have pierced” (Zechariah 12:10) — and Isaiah's Servant was “wounded for our transgressions” (Isaiah 53:5), where the word under “wounded” is chalal: properly, to bore through.
At the mouth of two witnesses the matter is established — the desert scroll and the old Greek keep the verb; Zechariah and Isaiah keep the event.
And the reading that takes the crucifixion out of the psalm is the one the tradition kept.

The case is not a point at all, but a letter — a letter the promise itself guards.
If the tradition was bold enough to settle even a letter against the elder witnesses, how much more easily a point?
The points touch no letter; they pass the jot-and-tittle pledge untried and slip through the fence of numbers with every scribal count intact — the one place a man could make his own point instead of God's, and leave the text looking untouched.

A command stands over exactly this.

Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it, that ye may keep the commandments of the LORD your God which I command you.

Kept as commentary, the points add nothing — they stand beside the word, a reading of men, weighed like any reading.
But elevated to Scripture itself — bound into the text and taught as though God had inspired them — they become an addition to the word in the plainest sense: a mark of man on every syllable of God's, “Add thou not unto his words, lest he reprove thee, and thou be found a liar” (Proverbs 30:6).

The command exists “that ye may keep the commandments” — the fence against adding exists for the sake of obedience, the same stake this chapter set at its start.
And His calendar sat under the same fence: the same community that fixed the vowels had long since traded the moon that is watched for a moon that is calculated — the appointed times this book reaches in the next part were guarded by the same social pressure.

This is no charge that the letters were lost; guarded by their numbers and answered by the scrolls from the desert, they held — held so well that the rare disputed letter stands exposed for weighing.
It is the vowel points that are on trial.
What the pointing added, by its own accounting, was a tradition of reading — and tradition is a category Scripture has already taught this book how to handle.

The Gentiles shall come unto thee from the ends of the earth, and shall say, Surely our fathers have inherited lies, vanity, and things wherein there is no profit.

Peter says the redeemed were bought out “from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers” (1 Peter 1:18); Jesus charges the scribes with “making the word of God of none effect through your tradition” (Mark 7:13).
None of that abolishes the scribes’ text — it ranks it.
The letters are the text; the pointing is the fathers’ reading of it — often right, worth hearing, and never the judge.

The ranking gives this book its rule, and it cuts both ways.
A reading the letters permit may stand even against the pointing — but it earns its place the way every reading in this book earns it: every occurrence gathered, witnesses required, counter-texts weighed.
The pointing gets a vote; it does not get a veto — and neither does the re-reading, until the letters and the witnesses agree.

The stakes are the same stakes this book has carried from its first chapter: obedience.
“Ye eat neither fat nor blood” is a standing command (Leviticus 3:17), spelled in milk's own letters — and the pointing a man trusts decides what obedience sets on his table.
A man who intends to keep the commandments exactly will want them exactly as they were written.
Dig past the points to the letters; that is where the best meat is cut.

There is one more thing the letters do — something no pointing can record and no translation can carry.
They rhyme in meaning.
The next chapter opens that second dimension: one verse, written once, that reads two ways and is true in both.

Determine whether the chapter confirms, refines, revises, or overturns your
prior commitment. In particular, assess its rule that the consonantal letters
are the written text while the pointing is an important reading tradition that
gets evidentiary weight but not automatic veto authority. Separate the
chapter's core textual rule from any historical polemic or downstream
application that is not necessary to that rule.

Do not discuss or anticipate any later disputed symbol. Return a final,
provider-specific commitment that can be frozen as a methodological premise
for subsequent experiments.
